statements.quote: We speak of "the information age" as if information became valuable only recently.
Information has been a **commodity** — something produced, shipped, priced, and traded — for centuries.
But a commodity is not just "valuable things"; a commodity is valuable *because it moves*.
It has producers, a price, a channel, and buyers.

So the question this chapter asks is not "when did information become important?" but **how was a *market* for it built** — because a market, with a flow, is the thing everything after it (the encyclopedia, the database, the web) runs on.
The first layer is the **market** itself.
statements.section: News becomes a commodity: the Fugger network (16th c.)

statements.quote: In the sixteenth century, in the banking city of Augsburg, the Fugger family ran one of Europe's largest information networks \cite[the Fugger news market, Wikipedia]{fuggernews}.
statements.section: News becomes a commodity: the Fugger network (16th c.)

statements.quote: Bankers and merchants lived on *information*: a rumor of war, a price in Venice, a ship lost at sea — any of these was money, and it was money that *decayed*.
statements.section: News becomes a commodity: the Fugger network (16th c.)

statements.quote: So the Fuggers ran a web of correspondents across Europe.
statements.section: News becomes a commodity: the Fugger network (16th c.)

statements.quote: A letter describing a significant event was copied and circulated as a news report; and a common device was a plain listing of current prices, the circulation of which quickened international trade \cite[News — early news networks, Wikipedia]{fuggernews}.
statements.section: News becomes a commodity: the Fugger network (16th c.)

statements.quote: This is the *Relation*, the German newssheet — and it is the first place we can point to news as a **product**: something a producer makes, ships out, and a buyer receives.
statements.section: News becomes a commodity: the Fugger network (16th c.)

statements.quote: Information has become the thing that is *sold*.

statements.quote: A commodity needs a **public**.
statements.section: The coffee-house public sphere

statements.quote: In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries the venue was the coffee house.
statements.section: The coffee-house public sphere

statements.quote: The sociologist \citeauthor{habermaspublicsphere} (\citeyear{habermaspublicsphere}) later named what was happening there: the **public sphere** — a space that was physically a coffee house in Britain, a salon in France, a reading society in Germany, where private individuals gathered to talk about *printed matter* as a shared reality \cite[the coffee-house public sphere, Habermas]{habermaspublicsphere}.
statements.section: The coffee-house public sphere

statements.quote: The authority is not in any single person's rank, title, or lineage.
statements.section: The coffee-house public sphere

statements.quote: It is in the **forum**: you argued a point, but you argued it to a public that had *read the same paper*.
statements.section: The coffee-house public sphere

statements.quote: Information stopped being a private possession in the head of the Fugger banker and became the raw material of a collective, argument-generating public.
statements.section: The coffee-house public sphere

statements.quote: The news sheet (the commodity) and the coffee house (the venue) are two halves of the same invention: a way for a *society* to share and contest what it knows.
statements.section: The coffee-house public sphere

statements.quote: The urge to gather *all* knowledge into one place is far older than the Enlightenment.
statements.section: Before the Encyclopédie: Isidore of Seville

statements.quote: Nearly eleven centuries before Diderot, in Visigothic Spain, the archbishop \cite[Isidore of Seville]{isidoreofseville} (c.
statements.section: Before the Encyclopédie: Isidore of Seville

statements.quote: 560–636) compiled the *\citetitle{etymologiae}* — a twenty-book encyclopedia that tried to capture the whole of ancient learning in a single ordered work.
statements.section: Before the Encyclopédie: Isidore of Seville

statements.quote: Its modern translators call it "arguably the most influential book, after the Bible, in the learned world of the Latin West for nearly a thousand years" \cite{etymologiae}.
statements.section: Before the Encyclopédie: Isidore of Seville

statements.quote: Isidore did not merely store the classics; he reorganized them.
statements.section: Before the Encyclopédie: Isidore of Seville

statements.quote: Drawing on hundreds of earlier authors — Pliny, Solinus, Servius, the church fathers — he sorted everything from grammar, rhetoric, and the mathematical *quadrivium* to medicine, law, animals, geography, and the making of furniture into twenty books, each a folder in one universal filing cabinet \cite{etymologiae}.
statements.section: Before the Encyclopédie: Isidore of Seville

statements.quote: The *Etymologiae* became *the* textbook of the Middle Ages, copied in nearly a thousand surviving manuscripts; so completely did it stand in for the originals that some classical works stopped being copied and were lost, surviving only as his excerpts \cite{etymologiae}.
statements.section: Before the Encyclopédie: Isidore of Seville

statements.quote: It is a fitting accident of history, then, that the Catholic Church has come to regard Isidore as the patron saint of the internet — and of computer users and programmers.
statements.section: Before the Encyclopédie: Isidore of Seville

statements.quote: The identification is best described as a popular, informal patronage: in the early 2000s Catholic internet groups and a Vatican media office promoted Isidore for the role, but no formal papal decree is documented, which is itself a very Isidorean sort of uncertainty (\cite[Shachtman, 2002]{wired2002isidore}).
statements.section: Before the Encyclopédie: Isidore of Seville

statements.quote: A seventh-century bishop who tried to put the whole world into twenty books is, at the very least, the right ancestor for the thing this chapter is about.
statements.section: Before the Encyclopédie: Isidore of Seville

statements.quote: If the coffee house was where information was *discussed*, the Encyclopédie was the great eighteenth-century attempt to **collect** it.
statements.section: The Encyclopédie: compiling everything at once

statements.quote: Between 1751 and 1772, \citeauthor{encyclopedie} and some hundred and forty contributors set out to put *all* known knowledge into a single work — the sciences, the arts, the trades — and, crucially, to **cross-reference** the articles to one another: a device the history of the book calls "a kind of precursor to the hyperlink" \cite[the Encyclopédie, Diderot & d'Alembert]{encyclopedie}.
statements.section: The Encyclopédie: compiling everything at once

statements.quote: The ambition was not merely to *store* knowledge but to *connect* it — and in doing so, to change how people thought.
statements.section: The Encyclopédie: compiling everything at once

statements.quote: This is the **corpus** in its first systematic form: a body of text, organized and internally linked, large enough that it becomes an object in its own right.
statements.section: The Encyclopédie: compiling everything at once

statements.quote: You can now point at "the Encyclopédie" the way you later point at "the web" — as a single, structured, interlinked thing.
statements.section: The Encyclopédie: compiling everything at once

statements.quote: Two centuries after Diderot, that object has a new name: the *training corpus* \cite[the Encyclopédie, Diderot & d'Alembert]{encyclopedie}.
statements.section: The Encyclopédie: compiling everything at once

statements.quote: Title page of the *Encyclopédie, ou dictionnaire raisonné des sciences, des arts et des métiers* (Diderot & d'Alembert, 1751).
statements.section: The Encyclopédie: compiling everything at once

statements.quote: The final layer is the one that was missing from the story for a hundred years, because it was almost lost.
statements.section: Paul Otlet and the Mundaneum: the library that wanted to be the world

statements.quote: In 1910 two Belgian lawyers — \cite[Paul Otlet]{paulotlet} and Henri La Fontaine — built the **Mundaneum** in Brussels \cite[the Mundaneum, Wikipedia]{mundaneum}.
statements.section: Paul Otlet and the Mundaneum: the library that wanted to be the world

statements.quote: It was a *documentation of the world*: every book, article, and fact they could collect reduced to a standardized index card, classified by the Universal Decimal Classification and **cross-indexed**, so that a single fact sat in many drawers at once.
statements.section: Paul Otlet and the Mundaneum: the library that wanted to be the world

statements.quote: At its height the building held more than twelve million cards — a physical model of the whole of human knowledge, *networked by index* \cite[the Mundaneum, Wikipedia]{mundaneum}.
statements.section: Paul Otlet and the Mundaneum: the library that wanted to be the world

statements.quote: In 1934 Otlet published the \cite[Traité de Documentation]{traitededocumentation}, and with it the vision that the next forty years would chase.
statements.section: 1934: the paper internet

statements.quote: He described a network of what he called "electric telescopes" — a *worldwide network* (a *réseau mondial*) of interlinked documents, held in a central repository, that anyone could consult from their own armchair: a moving image of the world, projected on a personal screen \cite[Wright, Cataloging the World (2014)]{catalogingtheworld}.
statements.section: 1934: the paper internet

statements.quote: He called that central repository the **mundotheque** — his word for a "world-library" that would display any document on demand, from anywhere \cite[the Mundaneum, Wikipedia]{mundaneum}.
statements.section: 1934: the paper internet

statements.quote: Read that again: a network of linked documents, *retrievable by query, from a distance, on demand*.
statements.section: 1934: the paper internet

statements.quote: In 1934, with paper cards and telegraph lines, Otlet was describing a **paper internet** — before the word "internet" was ever applied to a network of computers.
statements.section: 1934: the paper internet

statements.quote: His 1934 vision directly prefigured the *Memex* that Vannevar Bush would make famous a decade later, and the [World Wide Web](untold_history_iii.php) that came after that.
statements.section: 1934: the paper internet

statements.quote: This is the hinge the course has been building toward: the moment the *corpus* stops being a thing you read in a room and becomes a thing you **query from anywhere**.
statements.section: 1934: the paper internet

statements.quote: \marginfig{palais_mondial_1930.jpg}{Otlet and Henri La Fontaine at the gates of the Palais Mondial, 1930 — the physical home of the Mundaneum's twelve million cross-indexed cards.
statements.section: 1934: the paper internet

statements.quote: Step back, and this whole chapter is the slow construction of a **system for information**, in four layers — each a displaced prerequisite of the one you use today:
statements.section: The payoff: four layers, one system

statements.quote: * **A market** — news as a priced, shipped commodity (the Fugger network, 16th c.).
statements.section: The payoff: four layers, one system

statements.quote: * **A public** — a venue where the commodity is shared and argued (the coffee house, 17th–18th c.).
statements.section: The payoff: four layers, one system

statements.quote: * **A corpus** — the attempt to collect and cross-link all of it (Isidore's *Etymologiae*, 7th c.; the Encyclopédie, 1751–72).
statements.section: The payoff: four layers, one system

statements.quote: * **A network** — the attempt to make the whole of it retrievable on demand (Otlet's paper internet, 1934).
statements.section: The payoff: four layers, one system

statements.quote: The mapping onto the present is not decoration.
statements.section: The payoff: four layers, one system

statements.quote: A search engine is the coffee house made global.
statements.section: The payoff: four layers, one system

statements.quote: A [vector database](vectorsearch.php) is the Mundaneum's twelve million cards, now floating in a metric space and retrieved by similarity instead of by drawer.
statements.section: The payoff: four layers, one system

statements.quote: And the [training corpus](training_data.php) — the entire crawlable web that modern models are trained on — is the Encyclopédie's dream of *all knowledge, cross-referenced*, finally achieved at a scale Diderot could not have imagined.
statements.section: The payoff: four layers, one system

statements.quote: The next chapter, [The Untold History of AI](untold_history_iii.php), follows this arc to its end: Vannevar Bush, whose *Memex* of 1945 carried Otlet's "read the world from your armchair" vision into the age of electronics, and the chain that became the web.
statements.section: The payoff: four layers, one system

statements.quote: > Information became a **commodity** (the Fugger news market), then a **public** (the coffee house), then a **corpus** (the Encyclopédie), and finally a **network** — Otlet's Mundaneum and 1934 "paper internet," a Memex before Bush.
statements.section: The payoff: four layers, one system

statements.quote: Every layer is a displaced prerequisite of the retrieval system you use today.
statements.section: The payoff: four layers, one system
